card.title: Text
card.subtitle: a passage, checked out of the library
card.status_plain: In the library. The checkout for this passage was made by hand. The automatic checkout is not built yet.

what_it_is: The checkout is the library handing the method one passage to code: the exact words, with the address of where they sit in the corpus. It is the join between the library (what we hold) and the method (how we read it).
why_it_matters: The whole project reads from the library, so the library has to hold the real thing, sourced the right way. We build it only from public-domain texts and record every source. A copy scraped from a site like Bible Gateway is under copyright and untraceable. Ours is legal to quote, cite, and keep. That lets the library do three things a scrape cannot: use the words openly, track what we hold and what we are still missing (the library audits its own silence, by name), and grow a long-term corpus of primary meaning-making texts across traditions, including the ones thin in what language models were trained on. The checkout is the first link in that chain. If the method reads a loose retyped copy instead, it drifts. The copy we first coded flattened Mark's ending and dropped 'for they were afraid', the exact fear the reading turns on.

how_it_works.you ask for: a passage: a work, a chapter, an edition.
how_it_works.the library does: finds it, checks four things (it is in our collection, it is split into pieces, the wording is exact, we have permission to share), and returns a sealed package.
how_it_works.you get back: the verbatim passage with its address baked in.

the_contrast.coder_saw_paraphrase: They kept silent, telling no one anything.
the_contrast.corpus_verbatim: They went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.
the_contrast.plain: The retyped copy dropped 'trembling and astonishment' and 'for they were afraid', the exact fear the method needs to notice the women's silence. The checkout gives the real words back.

how_stored.plain: The book of Mark is one source (GUT-8268). The library splits it into 56 paragraph-pieces (level 4). There is no chapter object above them. So a passage is not a fixed size. It is a span of pieces, chosen by the goal.
passage_types: the resurrection: 2 pieces (paragraph 55 = 15:43 to 16:8, paragraph 56 = 16:9 to 20)
a single gloss on one passage: 1 piece
how_stored.this_checkout: This checkout composed 2 pieces, because the goal is the resurrection.

where_saved.plain: The words in this checkout are a copy. Everything the method builds on them saves to the corpus, in the same tables every text uses: the moves, the situating, the gaps, the glosses. One record ties them together for this passage, the text's home. It holds the checkout and points to each output, so all of Mark's coding sits in one findable place, joined by the checkout's address (source, passage, verse). Every text gets the same home, from the first one. The reading room reads it, the library folds results from it back into the corpus, and any later report or model reads the same store.

honest_limits: Mark exists in the library two ways (whole-chapter and verse-by-verse). We use the whole-chapter source and will remove the duplicate.
The automatic checkout (ask for any text, get a package) is not built. This is a worked example for Mark. The general version is WEMI Phase-1.
whats_next: Decompose (break the passage into moves) then Situate (the world the text came from).
